'''''Gossypium hirsutum''''', also known as '''upland cotton''' or '''Mexican cotton''', is the most widely planted species of [[Gossypium|cotton]] in the world. Globally, about 90% of all cotton production is of cultivars derived from this species.<ref>[https://www.yara.us/crop-nutrition/cotton/world-cotton-production/#:~:text=90%25%20of%20today's%20commercial%20cotton,most%20of%20their%20production%20domestically. World Cotton Production, Yara North America]</ref> In the United States, the world's largest exporter of cotton, it constitutes approximately 95% of all cotton production.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ers.usda.gov/topics/crops/cotton-wool/cotton-sector-at-a-glance/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190111184422/https://www.ers.usda.gov/topics/crops/cotton-wool/cotton-sector-at-a-glance/|archive-date=January 11, 2019|title=USDA ERS - Cotton Sector at a Glance|website=www.ers.usda.gov|access-date=2019-02-18}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Davenport |first=Coral |date=2023-02-18 |title=How Climate Change Is Making Tampons (and Lots of Other Stuff) More Expensive |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2023/02/18/climate/climate-change-cotton-tampons.html |access-date=2023-02-19 |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> It is native from Mexico to Ecuador and northeast Brazil, the [[Leeward Antilles]] in the Caribbean and the Pacific ([[Fiji]], [[Marianas]], [[Polynesia]] and [[Revillagigedo Islands]]).<ref>https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:30042843-2</ref> 

It is believed that ''Gossypium hirsutum'' was created when a wild Mexican cotton species mixed with the wild African species ''[[Gossypium herbaceum]]'' around 5–10 million years ago, producing a hybrid species with 4 pairs of chromosomes (totaling 52 chromosomes) via [[polyploidy]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Postrel |first1=Virginia |title=The Fabric of Civilization : How Textiles Made the World |date=2021 |publisher=BASIC BOOKS |isbn=9781541617629 |pages=26}}</ref>

The original native range of ''Gossyypium hirsutum'' centers on the [[Yucatán Peninsula]], where researchers have found the greatest genetic diversity among samples taken from the wild.<ref>[https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2607107123 "Genomic diversity and the domestication history of cotton Gossypium hirsutum", Ning et al, PNAS, May 18, 2026]</ref>

Archeological evidence from the [[Tehuacan Valley]] in Mexico shows the cultivation of this species as long ago as 3,500 BC, although there is as yet no evidence as to exactly where it may have been first domesticated.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Smith|first1=C. E.|last2=Stephens|first2=S. G.|doi=10.1007/BF02860076|title=Critical identification of Mexican archaeological cotton remains|journal=Economic Botany|volume=25|issue=2|page=160|year=1971|bibcode=1971EcBot..25..160S |s2cid=24273337}}</ref> This is the earliest evidence of cotton cultivation in the Americas found thus far.

''Gossypium hirsutum'' includes a number of varieties or cross-bred [[cultivar]]s with varying fiber lengths and tolerances to a number of growing conditions. The longer length varieties are called "long staple upland" and the shorter length varieties are referred to as "short staple upland". The long staple varieties are the most widely cultivated in commercial production.

Besides being fibre crops, ''Gossypium hirsutum'' and ''Gossypium herbaceum'' are the main species used to produce [[cottonseed oil]].

The [[Zuni people]] use this plant to make ceremonial garments,<ref>Stevenson, Matilda Coxe 1915 Ethnobotany of the Zuni Indians. SI-BAE Annual Report #30 (p. 77)</ref> and the fuzz is made into cords and used ceremonially.<ref>Stevenson, p.92</ref>
[[File:Gossypium hirsutum Florida.jpg|right|thumb|Flowers of ''Gossypium hirsutum'']]

This species shows [[extrafloral nectaries|extrafloral nectar]] production.<ref>Röse USR, Lewis J, Tumlinson JH. Extrafloral nectar from cotton (Gossypium hirsutum) as a food source for parasitic wasps. Functional Ecology 2006; 20:67-74.</ref>
